content: The assays available for diagnostic purposes include those for assessing immune function, growth hormones, sepsis, and arthritis. Additionally, specific assays are available for detecting infectious diseases such as HIV, hepatitis viruses (types A-C), cytomegalovirus (CMV), herpes simplex virus (HSV), syphilis, rubella, Trichomonas vaginalis and/or Mycoplasma genitalium (TV/MG), methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), West Nile virus (WNV), and COVID-19. The Roche cobas MTB and cobas MTB-RIF/INH assays are molecular diagnostic tools that may also be implemented by laboratories interested in running third-party molecular tests or laboratory-developed tests. These assays are designed for use with the Roche cobas 6800/8800 systems, which require significant infrastructure and dedicated laboratory spaces for sample preparation and amplification using real-time PCR. Automated sample preparation is possible with the cobas instrument, which must be regularly serviced and maintained. For digital data integration, diagnostic connectivity solutions and e-systems can be explored to align with the laboratory strengthening targets outlined in the End TB Strategy. Quality assurance systems for the cobas assays are similar to those of other moderate-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs). Similarly, the cobas MTB-RIF/INH assay requires validation for precision and accuracy in detecting drug resistance mutations. To prevent contamination, positive and negative controls must be included in each run, and laboratory spaces should be tested for contamination at least monthly. Laboratory technicians using the cobas 6800/8800 systems must be fully trained in automated DNA extraction, amplification, fluorescence detection, and reporting to troubleshoot and maintain the systems effectively. Clinicians and laboratory staff should also be trained to interpret resistance results for all included medicines. The Bruker-Hain FluoroType MTB and FluoroType MTBDR assays are real-time NAATs designed to detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) and resistance to rifampicin (RIF) and isoniazid (INH). These assays target specific genetic regions associated with drug resistance and offer both manual and automated DNA extraction options. The instruments used for amplification and detection include the FluoroCycler 12 and FluoroCycler XT. These assays are classified as moderate-complexity automated NAATs by the World Health Organization (WHO) and are recommended for use in centralized reference laboratories due to their high infrastructure requirements. The FluoroType assays perform well in diagnosing tuberculosis (TB) and detecting RIF and INH resistance compared to culture and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST). Results are automated via FluoroSoftware, which reports highand low-level INH resistance and identifies specific mutations. The assays are compatible with laboratory information management systems and can be integrated into diagnostic connectivity solutions. The Cepheid Xpert MTB/XDR test detects MTBC DNA and genomic mutations associated with resistance to INH, fluoroquinolones (FQs), ethionamide (ETH), and second-line injectable drugs (e.g., amikacin, kanamycin, capreomycin) in a single cartridge. This test is run on GeneXpert instruments with 10-color modules, which differ from the 6-color modules used for other Xpert tests. The Xpert MTB/XDR test is intended as a reflex test for TB specimens that are MTBC-positive. It performs well in detecting resistance to INH, FQs, ETH, and amikacin, with a limit of detection of 136 CFU/mL for unprocessed sputum and 86 CFU/mL for sputum sediment. The WHO recommends low-complexity automated NAATs like Xpert MTB/XDR for detecting drug resistance in bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB cases. These tests are particularly useful for detecting resistance to INH, FQs, ETH, and amikacin, rather than relying on culture-based phenotypic DST. The recommendations are based on evidence of diagnostic accuracy in sputum samples from adults with confirmed pulmonary TB, with extrapolation to adolescents and children. Operational considerations for implementing the Xpert MTB/XDR test include ensuring compatibility with 10-color GeneXpert modules, maintaining appropriate storage conditions for cartridges and reagents, and conducting quality assurance activities. Training for laboratory staff and clinicians should focus on interpreting resistance results for all included medicines. Additionally, countries should consider revising laboratory registers and reporting forms to accommodate the expanded set of drug-susceptibility results provided by this test.
